Coding 8 compared two means. Lecture A010 added two tests for other kinds of data, and this activity runs both: **one-way ANOVA** for a continuous response across three or more groups, and **chi-square** for counts in categories. Same recipe as always: H₀ as math, α first, look, check, test, conclude.

Part A uses Palmer Penguins. Part B uses the exact counts from the slides.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Which test? Match the data type (click to expand)

| Your data | Test | H₀ as math | R |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuous response, 2 groups | *t*-test (Welch, or paired) | μ₁ = μ₂ | `t.test()` |
| Continuous response, 3+ groups | One-way ANOVA, then Tukey HSD | μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = … | `aov()`, `TukeyHSD()` |
| Counts in categories, one variable vs. a predicted ratio | χ² goodness of fit | counts follow the ratio | `chisq.test(x, p = ...)` |
| Counts in categories, two variables | χ² test of independence | the variables are unrelated | `chisq.test(table)` |

Pick the test from the data type and the number of groups. The research question tells you which row you are in.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ANOVA and chi-square functions (click to expand)

| Function | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `aov(y ~ group, data = )` | Fits a one-way ANOVA; H₀ is that every group mean is equal | `aov(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguin_data)` |
| `summary(model)` | Prints the F statistic and its p-value | `summary(anova_model)` |
| `residuals(model)` | Each value minus its own group mean, one number per row | `residuals(anova_model)` |
| `shapiro.test(residuals(model))` | Normality check on the residuals, one check for the whole model | |
| `fligner.test(y ~ group, data = )` | Equal-variance check across groups; H₀ is equal variances | `fligner.test(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguin_data)` |
| `TukeyHSD(model)` | Every pairwise difference with the family-wise error rate held at α | `TukeyHSD(anova_model)` |
| `choose(k, 2)` | How many pairs k groups make | `choose(6, 2)` is 15 |
| `chisq.test(x, p = )` | Goodness of fit: observed counts vs. a predicted ratio | `chisq.test(c(428, 152), p = c(3/4, 1/4))` |
| `chisq.test(table)` | Independence: are two categorical variables related? | `chisq.test(infection_table)` |
| `matrix(..., nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)` | Builds a contingency table from counts | see step 15 |

`shapiro.test()`, `fligner.test()`, and `chisq.test()` all return the same kind of object as `t.test()`: pull pieces out with `$statistic`, `$parameter`, and `$p.value`.
:::

## Part A: One-way ANOVA

**Research question:** Does mean bill depth differ among Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins?

H₀: μ_Adelie = μ_Chinstrap = μ_Gentoo. Hₐ: at least one mean differs. One-way ANOVA, F statistic, α = 0.05. Then, if the ANOVA is significant, Tukey's HSD to see **which** species differ.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

1.  How many **factors** are in this analysis, and how many **levels**?
2.  What is the **response** variable?
3.  Why not run three *t*-tests (Adelie vs. Chinstrap, Adelie vs. Gentoo, Chinstrap vs. Gentoo)?

**Answers:** one factor (`species`) with three levels; `bill_depth_mm`; each test has a 5% false-positive rate, and the chances add up. Step 10 puts a number on it.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: box_species
```

```{webr}
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Layers are joined with `+`.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Keep the `ggplot()` call and add `geom_boxplot()` with `+`.")
} else if (!"GeomBoxplot" %in% layer_class(p, "geom")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but no boxes. Add `geom_boxplot()`.")
} else if (!exists("box_species", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Boxplot drawn. Save it as `box_species` with `<-`.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Three boxes. Gentoo sits lower; Adelie and Chinstrap overlap.")
}
```

Make a histogram of `bill_depth_mm` with one panel per species using `facet_wrap(~ species)`. Save it as `hist_species` and display it.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: hist_species
```

## Hint

Add `geom_histogram()`, then `facet_wrap(~ species)`. The slide did the same with `facet_wrap(~ feed)`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="hist_species"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
hist_species <- ggplot(penguin_data, aes(x = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ species)

```

Each species on its own looks roughly bell-shaped. Stacked together they would look bimodal, because Gentoo sits 3 mm lower. That is why ANOVA checks normality on the **residuals**, not on the pooled response.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: hist_species
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. `facet_wrap()` takes a formula: `~ species`.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Keep the `ggplot()` call and add `geom_histogram()` with `+`.")
} else if (!"StatBin" %in% layer_class(p, "stat")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but not a histogram. Add `geom_histogram()`.")
} else if (inherits(p$facet, "FacetNull")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Histogram drawn, but all three species are stacked in one panel. Add `facet_wrap(~ species)`.")
} else if (!exists("hist_species", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Faceted histogram drawn. Save it as `hist_species` with `<-`.")
```

### 5. Fit the ANOVA

Fit a one-way ANOVA of `bill_depth_mm` by `species` with `aov()`. Save the model as `anova_model` and print `summary(anova_model)`.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: anova_model
anova_model <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="anova_model"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Same formula shape as the two-sample *t*-test: response, tilde, grouping factor, `data =`.

``` r
fit <- aov(weight ~ feed, data = chickwts)
summary(fit)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="anova_model"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
anova_model <- aov(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguin_data)
summary(anova_model)
```

F = 360 on 2 and 339 df, p < 2 × 10⁻¹⁶. The spread of the three group means is enormous compared with the spread within groups.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: anova_model
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. The formula is `bill_depth_mm ~ species`, and the table goes in `data = penguin_data`.")
} else if (!exists("anova_model", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Save the model as `anova_model` with `<-`, then print `summary(anova_model)`.")
} else {
  am <- get("anova_model", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!inherits(am, "aov")) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`anova_model` should come from `aov()`, not `lm()` or `t.test()`.")
  } else {
    sm <- summary(am)[[1]]
    fval <- sm$`F value`[1]
    if (!is.na(fval) && abs(fval - 359.8) < 1) {
      list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
           message = "F = 360, p < 2e-16. At least one species mean differs. Which ones? Not yet.")
    } else {
      list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
           message = paste0("An ANOVA, but F = ", round(fval, 1), ". Use `bill_depth_mm ~ species` with `data = penguin_data`."))
    }
  }
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

F = 360, p < 2 × 10⁻¹⁶. What have you learned?

A.  Every species has a different mean bill depth\
B.  At least one species has a different mean bill depth\
C.  Gentoo bills are the shallowest

**Answer:** B. The F test says "at least one differs". It does not say which, and it does not rank them. That is Tukey's job in step 11.
:::

### 6. Add the residuals

A residual is each value minus its own group mean. `residuals(anova_model)` returns one per penguin, in the same row order as `penguin_data`. Add them as a column named `resid` with `mutate()` and save the result back as `penguin_data`.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: add_resid
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(bill_depth_mm))
anova_model <- aov(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguin_data)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: add_resid
penguin_data <- penguin_data |>

```

:::: {.hint exercise="add_resid"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`mutate()` can take a vector that is the same length as the table.

``` r
fit <- aov(weight ~ feed, data = chickwts)
chickwts |>
  mutate(resid = residuals(fit))
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="add_resid"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
penguin_data <- penguin_data |>
  mutate(resid = residuals(anova_model))
penguin_data
```

A new column. An Adelie with a 19.3 mm bill has a residual of about +1.0, because the Adelie mean is 18.3.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: add_resid
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Inside `mutate()` write `resid = residuals(anova_model)`.")
} else if (!exists("penguin_data", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Save the result back as `penguin_data` with `<-`.")
} else {
  pd <- get("penguin_data", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!is.data.frame(pd) || !"resid" %in% names(pd)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "No `resid` column yet. Add it with `mutate(resid = residuals(anova_model))`.")
  } else if (abs(mean(pd$resid)) < 1e-8 && abs(sd(pd$resid) - 1.118) < 0.05) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "`resid` added: 342 residuals that average zero. One normality check for the whole model.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "`resid` exists but does not look like the model residuals. Use `residuals(anova_model)`.")
  }
}
```

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: hist_resid
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
find_plot <- function(v, env) {
  if (inherits(v, "ggplot")) return(v)
  for (nm in rev(ls(env))) {
    o <- get(nm, envir = env)
    if (inherits(o, "ggplot")) return(o)
  }
  NULL
}
layer_class <- function(p, part) vapply(p$layers, function(l) class(l[[part]])[1], character(1))
plot_x <- function(p) {
  m <- c(as.list(p$mapping), unlist(lapply(p$layers, function(l) as.list(l$mapping)), recursive = FALSE))
  names(m) <- sub(".*\\.", "", names(m))
  if (is.null(m$x)) NULL else rlang::as_label(m$x)
}
p <- find_plot(.last_value, .envir_result)
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Layers are joined with `+`.")
} else if (is.null(p)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "No figure yet. Keep the `ggplot()` call and add `geom_histogram()` with `+`.")
} else if (!"StatBin" %in% layer_class(p, "stat")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "A figure, but not a histogram. Add `geom_histogram()`.")
} else if (!identical(plot_x(p), "resid")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
       message = "A histogram, but not of the residuals. Map `x = resid`.")
} else if (!exists("hist_resid", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Histogram drawn. Save it as `hist_resid` with `<-`.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "A single bell centered on zero. This is the picture the normality assumption is about.")
}
```

### 8. Shapiro-Wilk on the residuals

Run `shapiro.test()` on `residuals(anova_model)`. Save it as `shapiro_resid` and print it.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: shapiro_resid
shapiro_resid <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="shapiro_resid"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Either of these is the same vector:

``` r
shapiro.test(residuals(anova_model))
shapiro.test(penguin_data$resid)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="shapiro_resid"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
shapiro_resid <- shapiro.test(residuals(anova_model))
shapiro_resid
```

W = 0.992, p = 0.047. Just under 0.05. Read the callout below before you react.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: shapiro_resid
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. Pass one vector: `residuals(anova_model)`.")
} else if (!exists("shapiro_resid", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Save the result as `shapiro_resid` with `<-`, then print it.")
} else {
  sr <- get("shapiro_resid", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!inherits(sr, "htest") || is.null(sr$p.value)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`shapiro_resid` should be the output of `shapiro.test()`.")
  } else if (abs(sr$p.value - 0.0472) < 0.005) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "W = 0.992, p = 0.047. Borderline. With n = 342 Shapiro-Wilk flags departures too small to see.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("A Shapiro result, but p = ", signif(sr$p.value, 3), ". Test the residuals, not the raw bill depths."))
  }
}
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## p = 0.047 is not an order

The histogram is a clean bell. W = 0.992 is about as close to 1 as the statistic gets. The p-value is small because n = 342: with that many values, Shapiro-Wilk can detect a departure from normality far too small to matter. ANOVA is robust to this kind of departure when the groups are this large and this similar in shape.

Decision: proceed with the ANOVA and report both facts. "Residuals were approximately normal (histogram symmetric; Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.99, p = 0.047 with n = 342)." A test result is one piece of evidence, not the verdict. Coding 7 made the same point in the other direction, when p = 0.029 on 49 values turned out to be a mild skew that changed nothing.
:::

### 10. Why not three *t*-tests?

Three species make three pairs. If each pair gets its own *t*-test at α = 0.05, what is the chance of at least one false positive when H₀ is true for every pair? Compute `n_pairs` with `choose(3, 2)` and `p_false_positive` as `1 - 0.95^n_pairs`. Print both.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: false_positive
n_pairs <-
p_false_positive <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="false_positive"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`0.95^n` is the chance that all n tests stay quiet when there is nothing to find. One minus that is the chance at least one of them fires.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="false_positive"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
n_pairs <- choose(3, 2)
p_false_positive <- 1 - 0.95^n_pairs
n_pairs
p_false_positive
```

3 pairs, 14% chance of at least one false positive. For the six feeds in `chickwts` it is 15 pairs and 54%. Tukey's HSD keeps the rate for the **whole set** of comparisons at 5%.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: false_positive
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. `choose(3, 2)` counts the pairs; `^` raises to a power.")
} else if (!exists("n_pairs", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE) ||
           !exists("p_false_positive", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Create both `n_pairs` and `p_false_positive`.")
} else {
  np <- get("n_pairs", envir = .envir_result)
  pf <- get("p_false_positive", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!is.numeric(np) || length(np) != 1 || np != 3) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "`n_pairs` should be 3: `choose(3, 2)`.")
  } else if (!is.numeric(pf) || length(pf) != 1 || abs(pf - 0.142625) > 1e-4) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "`p_false_positive` should be `1 - 0.95^n_pairs`, about 0.14.")
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "Three tests, 14% chance of a false positive. Fifteen tests would be 54%.")
  }
}
```

### 11. Tukey's HSD

The ANOVA said at least one species differs. Run `TukeyHSD()` on `anova_model` to find out which. Save it as `tukey_result` and print it.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: tukey_result
tukey_result <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="tukey_result"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Pass the fitted model, not the data.

``` r
TukeyHSD(fit)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="tukey_result"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(anova_model)
tukey_result
```

Three rows, one per pair. `diff` is the difference in means, `lwr` and `upr` are a 95% family-wise confidence interval, and `p adj` is the p-value after correction. Chinstrap − Adelie: 0.07 mm, p adj = 0.89. Gentoo − Adelie: −3.36 mm, p adj < 0.0001. Gentoo − Chinstrap: −3.44 mm, p adj < 0.0001.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: tukey_result
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. `TukeyHSD()` takes the model object `anova_model`.")
} else if (!exists("tukey_result", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Save the result as `tukey_result` with `<-`, then print it.")
} else {
  tr <- get("tukey_result", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!inherits(tr, "TukeyHSD") || is.null(tr$species)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`tukey_result` should be `TukeyHSD(anova_model)`.")
  } else {
    padj <- tr$species[, "p adj"]
    if (abs(padj["Chinstrap-Adelie"] - 0.893) < 0.01 && padj["Gentoo-Adelie"] < 0.001) {
      list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
           message = "Three pairs. One is not significant (Chinstrap vs. Adelie); Gentoo differs from both.")
    } else {
      list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
           message = "A Tukey table, but the p-values do not match the bill-depth model. Run it on `anova_model`.")
    }
  }
}
```

### 12. Make the call

Using `tukey_result`, assign two logicals: `adelie_chinstrap_differ` (do Adelie and Chinstrap differ at α = 0.05?) and `gentoo_shallower` (is the Gentoo mean below both others, and significantly so?).

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: tukey_call
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(bill_depth_mm))
anova_model <- aov(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguin_data)
tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(anova_model)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: tukey_call
adelie_chinstrap_differ <-
gentoo_shallower <-
```

:::: {.hint exercise="tukey_call"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Read the `p adj` column and the sign of `diff` for the two Gentoo rows. `tukey_result$species` is the table as a matrix if you want to look at it directly.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="tukey_call"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
adelie_chinstrap_differ <- FALSE
gentoo_shallower <- TRUE
```

The overall ANOVA was significant, but only Gentoo stands apart. Adelie and Chinstrap bill depths are statistically indistinguishable (p adj = 0.89). Gentoo bills are about 3.4 mm shallower than both.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: tukey_call
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. `TRUE` and `FALSE` are written in all caps with no quotes.")
} else if (!exists("adelie_chinstrap_differ", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE) ||
           !exists("gentoo_shallower", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Assign both `adelie_chinstrap_differ` and `gentoo_shallower` to `TRUE` or `FALSE`.")
} else {
  a <- get("adelie_chinstrap_differ", envir = .envir_result)
  g <- get("gentoo_shallower", envir = .envir_result)
  ok <- function(x) is.logical(x) && length(x) == 1 && !is.na(x)
  if (!ok(a) || !ok(g)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "Both objects should be exactly `TRUE` or `FALSE`.")
  } else if (isTRUE(a)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "Chinstrap − Adelie has p adj = 0.89 and a 0.07 mm difference. They do not differ.")
  } else if (!isTRUE(g)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "Both Gentoo rows have negative `diff` and p adj < 0.0001. Gentoo is significantly shallower than both.")
  } else {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "Correct. One non-significant pair, and Gentoo shallower than both others.")
  }
}
```

## Part B: Chi-square

When the response is a **count in categories**, there is no mean to compare. Chi-square compares the counts you observed with the counts H₀ predicts. Two versions: **goodness of fit** (one categorical variable; expected counts come from a hypothesis) and **independence** (two categorical variables; expected counts assume the variables are unrelated).

### 13. Goodness of fit: Mendel's pea pods

All parents were heterozygous for pod colour and green is dominant, so H₀ predicts 3 green : 1 yellow in the F₂. Mendel observed 428 green and 152 yellow. Create `observed_counts` as a named vector and run `chisq.test()` with `p = c(3/4, 1/4)`. Save it as `chisq_gof` and print it.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: chisq_gof
observed_counts <- c(green = 428, yellow = 152)
chisq_gof <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="chisq_gof"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`p =` gives the predicted proportions, in the same order as the counts. They must add to 1.

``` r
chisq.test(c(50, 30, 20), p = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2))
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="chisq_gof"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
observed_counts <- c(green = 428, yellow = 152)
chisq_gof <- chisq.test(observed_counts, p = c(3/4, 1/4))
chisq_gof
```

χ² = 0.45, df = 1, p = 0.50. Expected counts were 435 and 145; the observed 428 and 152 are well within chance.
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: chisq_gof
#| check: true
had_error <- any(vapply(.evaluate_result, inherits, logical(1), "error"))
if (had_error) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "R stopped. Read the last line of the message. The proportions in `p =` must add to 1 and match the number of counts.")
} else if (!exists("chisq_gof", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
       message = "Save the result as `chisq_gof` with `<-`, then print it.")
} else {
  cg <- get("chisq_gof", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!inherits(cg, "htest") || !grepl("Chi-squared", cg$method)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`chisq_gof` should be the output of `chisq.test()`.")
  } else if (abs(unname(cg$statistic) - 131.3) < 1) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = "Without `p =`, `chisq.test()` tests a 1 : 1 ratio, which Mendel's data reject (p < 0.0001). Add `p = c(3/4, 1/4)` to test 3 : 1.")
  } else if (abs(unname(cg$statistic) - 0.4506) < 0.01) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "X-squared = 0.45, df = 1, p = 0.50. Same as the slide.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("A chi-square result, but X-squared = ", round(unname(cg$statistic), 2), ". Use the counts 428 and 152 with `p = c(3/4, 1/4)`."))
  }
}
```

### 15. Independence: lizard infection by habitat

Sixty lizards from an urban site and sixty from a forest site were scored infected or clean. The contingency table is built for you with `matrix()`. H₀: infection status is independent of habitat. Run `chisq.test()` on `infection_table` with `correct = FALSE`, as on the slide. Save it as `chisq_indep` and print it.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: chisq_indep
infection_table <- matrix(
  c(18, 42,
    33, 27),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(habitat = c("urban", "forest"),
                  status = c("infected", "clean")))
```

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
#| exercise: chisq_indep
infection_table <- matrix(
  c(18, 42,
    33, 27),
  nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(habitat = c("urban", "forest"),
                  status = c("infected", "clean")))
infection_table
chisq_indep <-

```

:::: {.hint exercise="chisq_indep"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Pass the whole table. No `p =`: the expected counts come from the row and column totals.

``` r
chisq.test(my_table, correct = FALSE)
```

`correct = FALSE` turns off a small-sample adjustment (Yates' correction) that R applies by default to 2 × 2 tables. With it, p = 0.0097 instead of 0.0056; same conclusion.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="chisq_indep"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
chisq_indep <- chisq.test(infection_table, correct = FALSE)
chisq_indep
```

χ² = 7.67, df = 1, p = 0.0056. Under independence each habitat would have 25.5 infected lizards; urban had 18 and forest had 33.
:::
::::

```{webr}

} else {

  if (!inherits(ci, "htest") || !grepl("Chi-squared", ci$method)) {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "info",
         message = "`chisq_indep` should be the output of `chisq.test()`.")
  } else if (abs(unname(ci$statistic) - 7.6726) < 0.01) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
         message = "X-squared = 7.67, df = 1, p = 0.0056. Same as the slide.")
  } else if (abs(unname(ci$statistic) - 6.6837) < 0.01) {
    list(correct = TRUE, type = "info",
         message = "X-squared = 6.68, p = 0.0097 with Yates' correction. Fine, and the slide used `correct = FALSE` (7.67, p = 0.0056). Same conclusion.")
  } else {
    list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning",
         message = paste0("A chi-square result, but X-squared = ", round(unname(ci$statistic), 2), ". Run it on `infection_table` as built above."))
  }
}
```

## 17. Recap: functions you practiced

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does each function do?

| Function | Role |
|---|---|
| `filter(!is.na(...))` | Drop rows with a missing response |
| `ggplot()` + `geom_boxplot()` | Compare a continuous response across factor levels |
| `geom_histogram()` + `facet_wrap(~ species)` | One distribution panel per level |
| `aov(y ~ group, data = )` | Fit a one-way ANOVA |
| `summary(anova_model)` | F statistic and p-value: does any mean differ? |
| `mutate(resid = residuals(anova_model))` | Attach residuals to the table |
| `geom_histogram()` on `resid` | Visual normality check for the whole model |
| `shapiro.test(residuals(anova_model))` | Formal normality check on the residuals |
| `fligner.test(y ~ group, data = )` | Equal-variance check |
| `choose(k, 2)` and `1 - 0.95^n` | How many pairs, and the family-wise false-positive rate |
| `TukeyHSD(anova_model)` | Which pairs differ, with the rate held at 5% |
| `chisq.test(x, p = )` | Goodness of fit against a predicted ratio |
| `chisq.test(table, correct = FALSE)` | Independence of two categorical variables |

If you can explain each row in your own words, you have covered **Coding Assignment 4, Part C** and the chi-square half of lecture A010.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Three things to say in your write-up

1.  **ANOVA says "at least one"; Tukey says which.** Reporting "Gentoo had the shallowest bills (ANOVA p < 0.001)" is wrong. The ANOVA p-value never tested Gentoo against anything. Cite the Tukey contrast: Gentoo − Adelie = −3.36 mm, 95% family-wise CI −3.68 to −3.04, p adj < 0.0001.
2.  **Checks are evidence, not verdicts.** The residual histogram was a clean bell; Shapiro-Wilk gave p = 0.047 on 342 values; Fligner gave p = 0.13. Report all three and your decision to proceed.
3.  **Chi-square shows association.** Forest lizards were infected more often (55% vs. 30%, χ² = 7.67, p = 0.0056). Nothing in the test says habitat is the cause.
:::

## 18. Transfer to Coding Assignment 4

On DataHub, Part C fits `aov(biomass_g ~ nitrogen, data = nitrogen_data)` with four nitrogen levels. The assignment asks for `plot(anova_model, which = 1)`, a base-R residuals-versus-fitted plot, instead of the residual histogram you built in step 7. Try it on the penguin model now so the picture is familiar:

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(bill_depth_mm))
anova_model <- aov(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguin_data)
plot(anova_model, which = 1)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Three vertical stripes, one per species mean, each a cloud of residuals centered on zero. Even spread across the stripes is the equal-variance assumption in picture form. Use only `which = 1`; the assignment does not ask you to interpret the other panels.
:::

Then `fligner.test()`, `TukeyHSD()`, and a write-up naming at least one significant and one non-significant nitrogen contrast. Same functions as steps 5 through 12.

## Keep playing

**Six feeds, fifteen pairs.** Run the lecture's ANOVA on `chickwts` and read the Tukey table from the slide.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
fit <- aov(weight ~ feed, data = chickwts)
summary(fit)
TukeyHSD(fit)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
F = 15.4, p = 6 × 10⁻¹⁰. Of the 15 pairs, 8 are significant. Sunflower and casein do not differ from each other (p adj = 0.9999) but beat horsebean, linseed, and soybean. That is the answer to "which feed would you give your chicks?"
:::

**When the variance check fails.** Try `body_mass_g` instead of bill depth.

```{webr}
#| envir: anova_lab
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_mass <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))
fligner.test(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguin_mass)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Fligner p = 0.01. Body mass varies more in Gentoo than in the other two species, so the equal-variance assumption fails. That is why this activity used bill depth. On the assignment, report the Fligner result either way; a failed check is a finding, not a failure.
:::

**Which test?** For each design, name the test.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

1.  Seedlings grown under four light treatments, 15 pots each, height measured after 30 days.
2.  For each of 200 nests, whether it was in a nest box or a natural cavity, and whether it fledged at least one chick.
3.  A bag of 500 M&Ms sorted by colour, compared with the proportions the company publishes.
4.  A one-way ANOVA on five diets gives p = 0.03, and a student reports "Diet 3 produced the heaviest mice (p = 0.03)." What is wrong?

**Answers:** (1) one-way ANOVA, then Tukey HSD if significant. (2) χ² test of independence: two categorical variables, one count per combination. (3) χ² goodness of fit: one categorical variable against a predicted ratio. (4) The ANOVA p-value does not test diet 3 against the others; a post-hoc test is needed before naming a winner.
:::
